Lecture 51

Laplace’s method and stationary phase

We prove leading formulas with explicit hypotheses and controlled remainders. We distinguish exponential localization from oscillatory cancellation and rescale the Gamma integral before applying a fixed-phase theorem.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Interpret absolute, relative and uniform error estimates at a stated limit.
  • Apply Laplace’s method with a strict gap and an integrable majorant.
  • Apply stationary phase at one nondegenerate interior stationary point.
  • Derive the leading real Stirling formula from the Gamma integral.

This lecture begins the study of asymptotic integrals. We seek the leading contribution to an integral with a large real parameter. We obtain a large-argument formula for J0J_0J0​ and prove that it has infinitely many positive zeros. We also approximate large factorials. The stages are orders and model integrals (Sections 51.1–51.2), Laplace’s method (Section 51.3), stationary phase (Section 51.4), then a comparison and the Gamma integral (Sections 51.5–51.6).

51.3 Laplace’s method

A real exponential gives greater weight to larger phase values. In the theorem below the maximum x0x_0x0​ of the phase is the dominant point, where the exponential weight is largest. A point x0x_0x0​ with f′(x0)=0f'(x_0)=0f′(x0​)=0 is a stationary point. It is nondegenerate if f′′(x0)≠0f''(x_0)\ne0f′′(x0​)=0. The gap hypothesis below controls the entire interval, including its ends.

51.4 Stationary phase

For an oscillatory integral the exponential has modulus one everywhere. Away from stationary points, integration by parts controls cancellation. Closed-interval differentiability below includes one-sided derivatives at the ends.

Proposition 51.10 (Zeros of J0J_0J0​). The function J0J_0J0​ has infinitely many positive zeros.

Proof. For integers n≥0n\ge0n≥0, the points Λ=(n+1/4)π\Lambda=(n+1/4)\piΛ=(n+1/4)π give cos⁡(Λ−π/4)=(−1)n\cos(\Lambda-\pi/4)=(-1)^ncos(Λ−π/4)=(−1)n. The error in (51.33), divided by 2/(πΛ)\sqrt{2/(\pi\Lambda)}2/(πΛ)​, tends to zero because ln⁡Λ/Λ→0\ln\Lambda/\sqrt\Lambda\to0lnΛ/Λ​→0. Indeed, ln⁡Λ=∫1Λ ⁣dt/t≤∫1Λt−3/4 ⁣dt=4(Λ1/4−1)\ln\Lambda=\int_1^\Lambda\dd t/t \le\int_1^\Lambda t^{-3/4}\dd t=4(\Lambda^{1/4}-1)lnΛ=∫1Λ​dt/t≤∫1Λ​t−3/4dt=4(Λ1/4−1) for Λ≥1\Lambda\ge1Λ≥1. Thus J0((n+1/4)π)J_0((n+1/4)\pi)J0​((n+1/4)π) has sign (−1)n(-1)^n(−1)n for all sufficiently large nnn. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem (GM 6) give a zero between each successive pair. These open intervals are disjoint, proving the claim. ■

This proves the existence assertion of Lecture 39’s theorem Zeros of Bessel functions for order zero. The zero-spacing limit stated there is not proved here.

Summary

A quadratic phase gives a Gaussian contribution for a real exponential and a Fresnel contribution for an imaginary exponential. The local formula needs a global estimate: a strict gap for Laplace’s method, and cancellation away from stationary points for stationary phase.

  • Orders: a limit and the dependence of constants are part of an error estimate. Relative errors require a nonzero approximation.

  • Laplace’s method: at a nondegenerate interior maximum, under the theorem’s other hypotheses (locally C3C^3C3 phase and C1C^1C1 amplitude, gap, weighted integrability), the leading term has an additive O ⁣(Λ−1)\bigO{\Lambda^{-1}}O(Λ−1) in the bracket multiplying eΛf(x0)\ee^{\Lambda f(x_0)}eΛf(x0​), for fixed data as Λ→+∞\Lambda\to+\inftyΛ→+∞.

  • Stationary phase: an exact quadratic coordinate and nonstationary integration by parts give the Fresnel phase factor and an additive O ⁣(Λ−1ln⁡Λ)\bigO{\Lambda^{-1}\ln\Lambda}O(Λ−1lnΛ) for fixed data in the theorem’s finite-interval class as Λ→+∞\Lambda\to+\inftyΛ→+∞.

  • Scaling: the moving Gamma maximum becomes fixed after t=Λxt=\Lambda xt=Λx, giving the real leading Stirling formula.

Lecture 52 reads the Gamma calculation in the complex plane and develops contour deformation for asymptotic integrals.
